article.title: Water Softener Not Using Salt? Causes and Fixes
article.summary: Water softener not using salt? Check the bypass, clock and settings, break a salt bridge or mush, clean the injector and test a manual regeneration.
article.body:
A water softener turns salt into brine to recharge its resin. If the salt level hasn't dropped in weeks and your water feels hard again, something is stopping that. Most causes are quick to check yourself. This guide covers salt-based softeners with a separate brine tank; use your manual for model-specific steps.

Affiliate disclosure: some links in this guide are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we'd use ourselves.

Safety: salt bags are heavy; lift with your legs. Unplug the softener and put it in bypass before you reach into the valve, and release pressure the way your manual shows before opening any cap.

Steps

  1. Confirm it's really not using salt

    Mark the salt level inside the brine tank with tape or a marker. Check it again after a week of normal water use, and test water from a cold kitchen faucet with hardness test strips. A level that hasn't moved plus hard water means the softener isn't making brine.

    Done right: you know the salt level is stuck and the water tests hard.

  2. Check the power, clock and bypass

    Make sure the softener is plugged in and the display is on. After a power outage, many units lose the time and regenerate at the wrong hour, so reset the clock. Then check the bypass valve on the head: it must be in the service position, not bypass.

    Done right: the display shows the correct time and water flows through the softener, not around it.

  3. Check the settings

    Look up the hardness and regeneration settings in your manual. If the hardness is set too low or regeneration is set too far apart, the softener rarely regenerates and uses little salt. Set the hardness to match a recent water test.

    Done right: the hardness setting matches your water test.

  4. Break up a salt bridge

    A salt bridge is a hard crust that forms above the water, so the tank looks full but the salt never reaches the water. Push a broom handle straight down through the salt in a few spots. If it stops on a hard layer, gently break it up without hitting the tank walls. See our water softener maintenance guide for the full routine.

    Done right: the handle slides all the way to the bottom of the tank.

  5. Clear salt mush from the bottom

    Salt mush is a thick sludge of recrystallized salt at the bottom of the tank that can block the brine well. If the handle hits mush, put the softener in bypass, scoop out the salt, vacuum out the water and sludge, and refill with fresh salt and a few inches of water, as your manual says.

    Done right: the bottom of the tank is clear, and the brine well is free of sludge.

  6. Clean the injector and screen

    The injector (venturi) is a small nozzle in the valve head that pulls brine out of the tank. With the softener in bypass and pressure released, remove the injector cap, then rinse the screen and nozzle in warm water and clear the openings with a soft brush or a toothpick. Put a little silicone grease on the O-rings and reassemble. Also check that the brine line isn't kinked or loose.

    Done right: the screen and nozzle are clean, and the brine line is firmly connected.

  7. Run a manual regeneration and watch

    Take the softener out of bypass and start a manual regeneration. During the brine draw, the water level in the brine tank should drop. Test your water the next day.

    Done right: the brine level drops during regeneration, the salt level falls over the next week, and the water tests soft.

Call a water treatment technician if: the softener won't start or stops partway through a regeneration, the brine level never drops after cleaning the injector, the control valve leaks, or the unit is 10 to 15 years old and the water stays hard.

FAQ

Why is my water softener not using salt?

The most common causes are a salt bridge, salt mush, a clogged injector or brine line, the softener sitting in bypass, or a clock or setting that keeps it from regenerating. A failed valve motor is less common.

What's the difference between a salt bridge and salt mush?

A salt bridge is a hard crust above the water with an empty gap below it. Salt mush is a sludge at the bottom of the tank. Both stop the softener from making brine.

Should there be water in my brine tank?

On most softeners, yes: a few inches of water sit in the bottom of the tank. Some models only add water before a regeneration. Check your manual for what's normal on yours.

Can I use rock salt in a water softener?

It's not recommended. Rock salt has more insoluble material that builds up as sludge. Use pellets or crystals made for water softeners.

How do I force my water softener to regenerate?

Most softeners have a button or dial for a manual or immediate regeneration. Check your manual for the exact steps on your model.

If your water softener isn't using salt, check that it's powered, out of bypass and set to the right hardness. Then push a broom handle through the salt to break any salt bridge, clear salt mush from the bottom, clean the injector screen, and run a manual regeneration to confirm the brine level drops.
